result.question: How recoverable is a failed or interrupted flash of the OP1w 4k (v1) firmware — is the bootloader separate and permanently resident, does the device enumerate under a distinct bootloader VID/PID, is the flash radio-mediated or cable-only, does the updater refuse to re-run at the same version, and what is the realistic worst case for a reimplemented Linux flasher?
result.answer:
SHORT VERDICT: recoverability looks unusually good — better than for most consumer-device DFU protocols — but one link in the chain cannot be proven from the host binary, and that link is the one that separates "retry it" from "brick".

=== 1. BOOTLOADER IS A DISTINCT USB IDENTITY — PROVEN ===

The single device-open helper is FUN_00401c00. It enumerates HID interfaces and requires, in this order:
  VID == 0x3367            (MOV EAX,0x3367; CMP word [EBP-0xc],AX  @ 00401CEA)
  PID == argument in EDX   (MOVZX EAX,word [EBP-0xa]; CMP EAX,[EBP-0x3c]  @ 00401CF5)
  HIDP_CAPS.UsagePage == 0xFF01  (@ 00401D4C)
  HIDP_CAPS.Usage == 0x02        (@ 00401D5A)
It then stores HIDD_ATTRIBUTES.VersionNumber into global 0x005BF978 as the displayed firmware version (@ 00401D80) and returns 1.

There are exactly 9 call sites to FUN_00401c00 in the whole .text, and every one is immediately preceded by a literal `MOV EDX,imm32`:
  0x1972 at 00404320, 00404345, 00404389, 00404A89, 00404AA5   — the APPLICATION
  0x1971 at 0040439E, 00404598, 0040460E, 00404695            — the BOOTLOADER
A byte scan of .text for `BA xx xx 00 00` with imm in 0x1000..0x2FFF returns only those nine plus unrelated constants. So the updater knows exactly two device identities: 3367:1972 and 3367:1971.

This upgrades PROTOCOL.md §8/§12's `[?]` inference to proven: cmd 0x0E's payload +4..+5 (0x1971 = mouse PID − 1) IS the bootloader PID. Update that tag from [?] to [BIN].

The device is closed and re-opened across the mode change (CloseHandle then open 0x1971 at 00404681-00404695, with retries every 300 ms up to 3000 ms), i.e. it genuinely re-enumerates. Two distinct PIDs from one device means two distinct enumerating programs, each with its own descriptors.

=== 2. THE UPDATER HAS AN EXPLICIT "ALREADY IN THE BOOTLOADER" RECOVERY PATH — PROVEN ===

This is the strongest single finding for your question. In the button handler FUN_004040f0:
  00404384  MOV EDX,0x1972 ; CALL 00401c00 ; if EAX==1 -> JZ 0040444A
            -> read version, AfxBeginThread(FUN_00403f00) -> FUN_004044b0 = FULL sequence (enter bootloader, then flash)
  00404399  MOV EDX,0x1971 ; CALL 00401c00 ; if EAX==1
            -> FUN_0040e394(FUN_00403f10,...) -> FUN_00404780 = FLASH ONLY, skipping the enter-bootloader step

So: if the updater cannot find the mouse as the application but does find it as the bootloader, it goes straight to flashing. A vendor writes that branch only because devices do end up stranded in the bootloader and must be recoverable by re-running the tool.

Corroborating: on a block-write failure the tool aborts after 5 attempts (70 ms apart) with "send block data request failed" and does nothing to clean up (00404971-00404B0E). That is only a sane design if re-running recovers.

Also, even when the enter-bootloader command itself appears to fail after 5 attempts, the tool still closes the handle and probes 0x1971 (00404585-00404598) before declaring "send bldr request failed".

=== 3. CABLE ONLY — NO RADIO PATH — PROVEN ===

The dongle PID 0x1970 is never passed to the open helper. Per PROTOCOL.md §10/§12, 0x1972 is the OP1w 4k v1 mouse's own identity when cabled; 0x1970 is the dongle shared by all four wireless models. The updater talks only to 0x1972 and 0x1971.

Supporting detail: none of the wireless-specific machinery appears — no 0x0F target probe, no 0x0E mouse-info, no 0xB4 battery, and the enter-bootloader command carries target byte 0x00, not 0x0F ("mouse via dongle"). Dongle firmware is a separate product (the "Endgame Gear 4k Dongle Firmware Updater" embedded in the v2 config tool, which uses a different bootloader vendor 0x22D4 with PIDs 0x1502/0x1503 — I confirmed those literals in the v1.04 config tool at file offsets 0x17FFB8/0x17FFBD).

Consequence: the much worse failure mode you were worried about — losing the 2.4 GHz link mid-write — does not exist on this path. The mouse must be plugged in.

=== 4. NO VERSION GATING — PROVEN — SO THE CAPTURE IS REPEATABLE ===

At 0040444A the tool calls FUN_00401e00 (which just reads global 0x5BF978, i.e. bcdDevice from HidD_GetAttributes), converts it (MOVZX / CVTDQ2PS / DIVSS [0059B320] / CVTPS2PD), formats "Mouse firmware current version %.2f", writes it to the status label, and then at 0040448C-0040449A unconditionally does PUSH 0,0,0,0 / PUSH EDI / PUSH 0x403f00 / CALL 0040e394 (AfxBeginThread).

There is no CMP or TEST on the version value anywhere between the read and the thread start. The version is displayed and discarded. There is also no "already up to date" string anywhere in the binary.

FUN_004040f0 has no direct callers; it is reached through the MFC message map entry at file offset 0x19975C: nMessage=0x0111 (WM_COMMAND), nCode=0, nID=nLastID=0x03E9 (1001), nSig=0x3A, pfn=0x004040F0 — i.e. the "Update Firmware" button. So nothing happens until the button is clicked, and then it always flashes.

Practical upshot: you can re-run the capture as many times as you like at the same version. You do not get one shot at the capture; you get one shot at each capture being clean. (And 1.08 -> 1.10 is a real upgrade anyway.)

=== 5. THE PROTOCOL, FOR THE SAFETY ARGUMENT ===

All requests are HidD_SetFeature/HidD_GetFeature with length EDX=0x411 (1041 bytes) on report 0xA0, i.e. the same bulk report the config protocol uses. Payload begins at +16, exactly as PROTOCOL.md documents. Status byte is at response +1; 0x01 = OK. Note the bootloader's busy code is 0x04, not the config protocol's 0x03 (FUN_00401f50 retries while [buf+1]==0x04, increasing sleep, up to 1000 ms).

Sequence (FUN_004044b0 then FUN_00404780):
  a) enter bootloader: A0 3A 00 00 | 00 5A A5 32 | zeros to 1041
     (MOV dword [ebp+fbe8],0x3aa0 @ 004044F7; MOV dword [ebp+fbec],0x32a55a00 @ 00404506)
     A magic unlock value, not normal framing. 5 attempts, sleeps of attempt*20 ms.
  b) CloseHandle; open 3367:1971, retry to 3000 ms; else "Open bldr device request failed"
  c) Sleep 1000; echo test: A0 01 01 00 with 1024 bytes of payload (the first firmware block, LEA EDX,[EBX+0x260] @ 00404623), device echoes it back, tool byte-compares response +16.. against what it sent (FUN_00402790). A pure loopback link test that writes nothing.
  d) Sleep 1000; start: A0 03 00 00, payload +16 = u8 block count (MOV BL,byte [EDI+0x25c] @ 004047C4 — note only the LOW BYTE), payload +17..+20 = u32le from dialog member [EDI+0x3EA60]. Requires response status 0x01.
  e) 205 x block data: A0 06 00 00, payload +16..+1039 = 1024 firmware bytes, and at buffer +4..+7 a CHECKSUM (FUN_00402640): a 16-bit accumulating sum of the 1024 payload bytes, loop over indices 0x10..0x40F, stored as a dword. 5 attempts per block, 70 ms apart; 70 ms between blocks.
  f) complete: A0 09 00 00. Requires status 0x01.
  g) open 3367:1972, retry every 500 ms up to 5000 ms. If it never comes back -> "Update failed, try again" (L at 0x0059B0DC).
  h) On success: A1 13 00 00 as a 64-byte report (MOV dword [EBP-0x50],0x13a1 @ 00404C01; MOV EDX,0x40 @ 00404C10), Sleep 1080 ms, read back. Command 0x13 is FACTORY RESET per PROTOCOL.md §3 — the updater wipes the user's configuration after flashing.

Two safety nets exist in the protocol itself: the per-block 16-bit checksum (a corrupt block is rejected, not written) and the pre-flash echo loopback.

=== 6. THE PAYLOAD ===

Two PE resources of type "FWFILE", language 2052, each exactly 0x33400 = 209,920 bytes:
  id 134 (0x86) at file offset 0x001D29E8, sha256 ad612be22f77907162429e1053a6fad5...
  id 135 (0x87) at file offset 0x00205DE8, sha256 e64312019946b4b5607b59f115f3d63a...

Only 134 is used: FindResourceW(NULL, 134, L"FWFILE") — the sole `PUSH 0x86` in the binary, at 00404195, and the only reference to L"FWFILE" (0x0059ADF0), from 00404190. There is no `PUSH 0x87` anywhere. Resource 135 is not reachable from any code path in this executable. What it is for is UNKNOWN.

FUN_004040f0 then: nblocks = SizeofResource >> 10 (205), remainder = size % 1024 (0), LoadResource, LockResource, and a plain unrolled dword copy into the dialog buffer at [this+0x260]. THERE IS NO DECRYPTION, DECOMPRESSION OR TRANSFORMATION ANYWHERE BETWEEN LockResource AND HidD_SetFeature. The resource bytes go to the device verbatim; the bootloader decrypts them.

Structure of the encrypted image (205 records of 1024 bytes):
  records 0..132   unique
  records 133..203 71 records, all byte-identical
  record 204       unique, differs from the filler
Within the filler record, all 64 of its 16-byte blocks are distinct. So the transform is position-dependent inside a 1024-byte record and position-independent across records — a 1024-byte-period keystream, not 16-byte ECB. The two images share zero records, not even the filler, so they are keyed differently or their filler plaintexts differ.

For feasibility this is good news (no key needed). For safety it is bad news: you cannot inspect, validate, version-check or model-check the payload. Record 204 is plausibly a trailer/CRC/version block, but that is SPECULATIVE.

The dialog buffer is 0x3E800 = 250 KB (0x260 + 0x3E800 = 0x3EA60, the next member), so 205 KB of firmware fits with 45 KB unused.

=== 7. IS THE BOOTLOADER OVERWRITTEN? — UNKNOWN, PROBABLY NOT ===

I cannot settle this from the host binary. What I can say:

Arguments it survives:
 - It has its own USB identity (0x1971) with its own descriptors — it is separate firmware, not a mode of the app.
 - The updater's recovery branch (section 2) only makes sense if it persists and enumerates.
 - The "start" command carries a block COUNT but no base address, so the write window is fixed inside the bootloader. Vendors do not place that window over the bootloader.
 - After "complete" the bootloader must still be running to hand control back to the app.
 - The image's last 72 KB is uniform filler plus one distinct record. If the bootloader lived at the top of flash you would expect real code there, not filler. (Weak.)

Residual risk I cannot close:
 - The only PROVEN entry into the bootloader is command A0 3A handled by the RUNNING APPLICATION. If a half-written app does not run, recovery depends on the bootloader deciding on its own to stay in DFU mode — e.g. because it cleared an app-validity marker before the first erase. That is the standard pattern and the updater's 0x1971 probe strongly implies it, but it is not proven.
 - Whether the device validates the decrypted image before jumping to it (a whole-image CRC in record 204?) is unknown.
 - What the u32 at start-payload +17 means is unknown. A byte scan for the displacement `60 EA 03 00` finds exactly ONE reference in the whole .text — the READ at 004047EA. No write was found. Either that member is uninitialised (and the device ignores it) or it is written through an addressing form my scan missed. If it IS a length or image checksum and a reimplementation gets it wrong, that matters.

=== 8. REALISTIC WORST CASE FOR A REIMPLEMENTED LINUX FLASHER ===

Ranked by likelihood:
 1. Most likely failure: a block is rejected (bad checksum/framing) or a response is misread, the tool aborts mid-flash, device sits at 3367:1971. Recover by running the Windows updater, which handles exactly this state. Cost: a Windows VM. NOT a brick.
 2. You send resource 135 instead of 134. Best case the bootloader's decryption or CRC rejects it. Worst case you write a valid-looking but wrong image. Unknown which.
 3. Unplugged / kernel reset / hidraw hiccup mid-flash. Same as (1) if the bootloader persists; a hard brick if it does not. This is the tail risk that cannot be quantified from static analysis.
 4. WORST AVOIDABLE MISTAKE, and the one I would actually worry about: sending A0 3A to the wrong device. The bootloader, the mouse application and the DONGLE all expose the same vendor collection 0xFF01/0x02 and the same report IDs 0xA0/0xA1. A Linux tool that selects its hidraw node by usage page alone — which is what PROTOCOL.md §1 correctly recommends for the CONFIG tool — can attach to 3367:1970 (the dongle) and start streaming 205 KB of mouse firmware at it. The dongle is a different chip with a different bootloader vendor (0x22D4) and is updated by a different tool. Bricking the dongle bricks all wireless use of the mouse. The existing egg::Device device-selection logic is therefore NOT safe to reuse for flashing without an additional hard gate.
 5. True unrecoverable brick requires the bootloader to be erased or to not persist. No evidence that it is; no proof that it isn't.

=== 9. WHAT THE ONE WINDOWS CAPTURE MUST NAIL (in priority order) ===

 1. The bootloader device itself: full device + configuration + HID REPORT DESCRIPTOR for 3367:1971. Without its report descriptor a Linux tool cannot reliably pick the right hidraw node or know the feature-report sizes. This is the item you cannot derive statically and cannot get any other way.
 2. Byte-compare the first outgoing block against record 0 of resource 134 (file offset 0x001D29E8, first bytes b2 06 aa d6 5b ca 25 f8). If they match, "stream the resource verbatim" is proven end to end, and that is the whole feasibility claim.
 3. The actual bytes of the start request — settle whether +17..+20 is garbage or meaningful.
 4. Per-block responses: status byte, and whether the device echoes the checksum or a block index.
 5. The complete response, the re-enumeration back to 3367:1972, and the new bcdDevice (expect 110 = 0x6E for v1.10).
 6. Real inter-command timing (the coded sleeps are 30/70/150/200/500/1000/1080 ms).
 7. Confirm the trailing A1 13 factory reset.

Do NOT deliberately interrupt the flash to test recoverability during this capture. Get one clean end-to-end trace first.
evidence: FUN_00401c00 (device open): VID gate `MOV EAX,0x3367; CMP word ptr [EBP + -0xc],AX` at 00401CEA-00401CEF; PID gate `MOVZX EAX,word ptr [EBP + -0xa]; CMP EAX,dword ptr [EBP + -0x3c]` at 00401CF5-00401CF9 where [EBP-0x3c] is the EDX argument saved at 00401C18; usage-page gate `MOV EAX,0xff01; CMP word ptr [0x005bf9b2],AX` at 00401D4C; usage gate `CMP word ptr [0x005bf9b0],0x2` at 00401D5A; version capture `MOVZX EAX,word ptr [EBP + -0x8]; MOV [0x005bf978],EAX` at 00401D80-00401D87 (HIDD_ATTRIBUTES.VersionNumber = bcdDevice)

All 9 call sites of FUN_00401c00, each with its immediately preceding PID literal: 00404320/00404345/00404389 (MOV EDX,0x1972), 0040439E (MOV EDX,0x1971), 00404598 (0x1971), 0040460E (0x1971), 00404695 (0x1971), 00404A89 (0x1972), 00404AA5 (0x1972). A scan of the whole .text (RAW 0x400, len 0x165200, VA 0x401000) for `BA xx xx 00 00` with imm in 0x1000..0x2FFF yields only these plus unrelated values (0x29F8, 0x1460, 0x2B90, 0x1040, 0x17E0, 0x1000). Dongle PID 0x1970 is never an argument.

Recovery branch in FUN_004040f0: `00404384 MOV EDX,0x1972 / 00404389 CALL 0x00401c00 / 0040438E CMP EAX,0x1 / 00404391 JZ 0x0040444a` (full sequence via FUN_00403f00 -> FUN_004044b0) versus `00404399 MOV EDX,0x1971 / 0040439E CALL 0x00401c00 / if EAX==1 -> PUSH 0x403f10 / CALL 0x0040e394` (flash-only via FUN_00403f10 -> FUN_00404780, skipping the enter-bootloader step).

No version gating: 0040444A CALL 0x00401e00 (version read) -> 0040444F MOVZX EAX,AX -> 00404455 MOVD XMM0,EAX / 0040445C CVTDQ2PS / 0040445F DIVSS XMM0,[0x0059b320] / 00404467 CVTPS2PD -> 0040446F PUSH 0x59ae70 (L"Mouse firmware current version %.2f") / 00404475 CALL 0x00402110 -> 00404487 CALL 0x00416e1f (set status text) -> 0040448C-0040449A PUSH 0,0,0,0 / PUSH EDI / PUSH 0x403f00 / CALL 0x0040e394. No CMP or TEST on the version between the read and the thread start; no "already up to date" string in the binary.

MFC message map entry at file offset 0x0019975C: `11 01 00 00 | 00 00 00 00 | e9 03 00 00 | e9 03 00 00 | 3a 00 00 00 | f0 40 40 00` = WM_COMMAND(0x0111), nCode 0, nID=nLastID=0x03E9 (1001), nSig 0x3A, pfn 0x004040F0 — so FUN_004040f0 is the "Update Firmware" button handler, not a startup path.

Enter-bootloader request, FUN_004044b0: `004044F7 MOV dword ptr [EBP + 0xfffffbe8],0x3aa0` and `00404506 MOV dword ptr [EBP + 0xfffffbec],0x32a55a00`, buffer zeroed from +8 for 0x409, `MOV EDX,0x411` (1041), `LEA ECX,[EBP+0xfffffbe8]`, CALL 00401eb0. On the wire: A0 3A 00 00 | 00 5A A5 32 | zeros. Then CloseHandle at 00404585/00404681 and open 0x1971 at 00404593/00404690 with `ADD ESI,0x12c` retries to 0xbb8 (3000 ms), failing at ESI==0xa8c with L"Open bldr device request failed" (0x0059AF10) or L"send bldr request failed" (0x0059AEDC).

Start request, FUN_00404780 at 004047C4-0040483B: buffer base [EBP+0xfffffb5c]; `MOV dword ptr [EBP+0xfffffb5c],0x3a0` (A0 03 00 00), `MOV dword ptr [EBP+0xfffffb60],0x0`, MOVQ of zeroed XMM0 into +8; `MOV BL,byte ptr [EDI + 0x25c]` (block count, LOW BYTE ONLY) stored at +0x10; the dword at [EDI+0x3ea60] split little-endian into +0x11..+0x14; memset 0x3fc from +0x15; `MOV EDX,0x411`; CALL 00401eb0. Response check `CMP byte ptr [EBP+0xfffff749],AL` (status +1 == 1) at 00404885.

Per-block checksum, FUN_00402640: `local_41c[0]=0xa0; local_41c[1]=6;` then 0x100 dwords (1024 B) copied to buffer +0x10, then a loop from index 0x10 adding four bytes per iteration while index < 0x410, accumulating into a ushort, result stored at buffer +4. So a 16-bit additive sum over exactly the 1024 payload bytes, at report offset +4..+7. Followed by write, Sleep(0x1e)=30 ms, then read with buf[0]=0xa0.

Block loop, 00404925-004049EA: src = [EDI+0x260] + i*0x400 (`ADD EAX,0x400` at 004049CD), `CALL 0x00402640` at 00404965, up to 5 attempts (`CMP ESI,0x5 / JGE 0x00404afc`) with Sleep(0x46)=70 ms, failure -> PUSH 0x59afc4 (L"send block data request failed").

Complete + return-to-application, 004049F0-00404AC6: `MOV dword ptr [EBP+0xfffffb5c],0x9a0` (A0 09 00 00), EDX=0x411, write, Sleep(0x96)=150 ms, read, require `CMP byte ptr [EBP+0xfffff749],0x1`; then `MOV EDX,0x1972 / CALL 0x00401c00` at 00404A84/00404AA0 with `ADD ESI,0x1f4` retries to 0x1388 (5000 ms); on failure PUSH 0x59b0dc = L"Update failed, try again".

Post-flash factory reset: `00404C01 MOV dword ptr [EBP + -0x50],0x13a1` (A1 13 00 00) with `00404C10 MOV EDX,0x40` (64-byte report 0xA1), then Sleep(0x438)=1080 ms and a read-back with buf[0]=0xA1. Command 0x13 is factory reset per PROTOCOL.md section 3 — the user's configuration is wiped by a successful update.

Echo/loopback test, FUN_00402790: `local_41c = 0x101a0` (A0 01 01 00), memcpy of 0x400 bytes into +0x10 from EDX, which the caller sets with `LEA EDX,[EBX + 0x260]` at 004045CE/00404623 (the first firmware block); after the read it byte-compares response +0x10.. against the sent payload for 1023 bytes. Writes nothing to flash.

Bootloader busy code differs from the config protocol, FUN_00401f50: retry loop is entered on `*(char *)(param_1 + 1) == '\x04'` (status 0x04), sleeping in +100 ms steps up to 1000 ms, exiting when status becomes 0x01. The config protocol's busy code is 0x03 (PROTOCOL.md section 2). Write helper FUN_00401eb0 uses the same GetLastError set as the config tool (0x15, 0x17, 0x1D, 0x57, 0x65B), 4 attempts, Sleep(0x32)=50 ms.

PE resource directory of the updater: two leaves of type "FWFILE", language 2052 — id 134 at dataRVA 0x001D91E8 / file offset 0x001D29E8, size 0x33400 (209,920); id 135 at dataRVA 0x0020C5E8 / file offset 0x00205DE8, same size. .rsrc is VA 0x001C0000 / RAW 0x001B9800 / size 0x00083380.

Only resource 134 is reachable: `00404195 PUSH 0x86` is the single occurrence of that immediate, feeding FindResourceW(NULL, 134, L"FWFILE"); L"FWFILE" lives at 0x0059ADF0 and has exactly one reference, from 00404190. No `PUSH 0x87` exists anywhere in the binary. Resource 135 is unreachable from this executable.

No transformation of the payload, FUN_004040f0 after LoadResource/LockResource: `*(DWORD *)(param_1 + 0x25c) = DVar6 >> 10` (nblocks = 205), remainder `DVar6 + (DVar6 >> 10) * -0x400` = 0, then a plain unrolled 4-bytes-at-a-time copy of the locked resource into the buffer at param_1+0x260. No decrypt, no decompress, no CRC recompute between LockResource and HidD_SetFeature.

Encrypted-image structure (209,920 bytes = 205 x 1024, both resources): records 0..132 unique; records 133..203 are 71 byte-identical records; record 204 unique and different from the filler. The filler repeats with period exactly 0x400 starting at 0x21400. Within the filler record all 64 of its 16-byte blocks are distinct, so the transform is position-dependent inside a 1024-byte record but position-independent across records — a 1024-byte-period keystream, not 16-byte ECB. Shannon entropy 7.979 bits/byte; all 256 byte values present; ~741 zero bytes.

The two payloads share nothing: 0 of 205 records match at the same index, and 0 records of resource 134 appear anywhere in resource 135 — including the filler record (134 filler sha256 904f4f03..., 135 filler sha256 f56d4755...). So the two images are keyed differently or their filler plaintexts differ. No plaintext version, magic or header is visible in either.

Dialog buffer sizing: the firmware buffer at [this+0x260] and the start-command dword at [this+0x3EA60] are adjacent — 0x3EA60 - 0x260 = 0x3E800 = 256,000 bytes (250 KB). A byte scan of .text for the displacement `60 EA 03 00` finds exactly one hit, 004047EA, which is the READ. No write to that member was found, so it is plausibly uninitialised and ignored by the device — but this is not proven, since a write could use an addressing form the scan missed.

Neither OP1w 4k configuration tool contains a firmware payload or bootloader strings: a UTF-16 scan of Endgame_Gear_OP1w_4k_Configuration_Tool_v1.04-fec5b994.exe and _v1.03.exe for "FWFILE" and "bldr" returns zero hits in both. The ~527 KB size delta versus the updater is the two 205 KB payloads plus the flash code.

Dongle bootloader is a different vendor entirely: in Endgame_Gear_OP1w_4k_Configuration_Tool_v1.04-fec5b994.exe, `PUSH 0x1503` at file offset 0x17FFB8 followed by `PUSH 0x22D4` at 0x17FFBD, plus further 0x1502/0x1503 pushes through 0x186000 — inside the embedded dongle-updater PE. So mouse bootloader = 3367:1971, dongle bootloader = 22D4:1502/1503, and they are flashed by different tools.

Error-string inventory and their referencing functions (from string xrefs): L"Loading firmware file failed" 0x00199400, L"Read firmware file failed" 0x0019943C, L"Mouse firmware current version %.2f" 0x00199470 (ref 0040446F in FUN_004040f0), L"Device not found" 0x001994B8, L"send bldr request failed" 0x001994DC (ref 004046EE), L"Open bldr device request failed" 0x00199510 (ref 004046D4), L"send echo request failed" 0x00199550 (ref 00404654), L"send bldr start request failed" 0x00199584 (ref 004048BB), L"send block data request failed" 0x001995C4 (ref 00404B09), L"send bldr complete request failed" 0x00199608 (ref 00404D4A), L"Firmware update successful! ..." 0x00199658, L"Update failed, try again" 0x001996DC. All file offsets; the .rdata mapping is VA = 0x400000 + 0x167000 + (fileoff - 0x165600).
result.risk_note:
Brick risk is LOWER than I expected going in, and the residual risk is concentrated in places that are easy to get wrong in a reimplementation rather than in the flash mechanics.

What genuinely reduces the risk, all proven from the binary: the bootloader has its own USB identity (3367:1971) so a stranded device is visible and addressable; the vendor updater contains an explicit code path that flashes a device found already in the bootloader, which is a recovery tool you get for free and should keep available; the path is USB-cable-only, so there is no radio link to lose mid-write; every block carries a 16-bit checksum so a corrupted block is rejected rather than written; there is a pre-flash echo loopback test; and there is no version gate, so re-running is always allowed and captures are repeatable.

What is NOT established, and what an honest decision has to price in: (1) whether the bootloader is inside or outside the fixed write window is unknown from the host side — the start command sends only a block count, no base address, so the window is chosen device-side and I cannot see it; (2) the only PROVEN way into the bootloader is command A0 3A handled by the running application, so recovery from a half-written app depends on the bootloader autonomously staying in DFU mode, which the updater's 0x1971 probe strongly implies but does not prove; (3) whether the device validates the decrypted image before jumping to it is unknown; (4) the meaning of the u32 at start-payload +17 is unknown (one read reference, no write found).

The payload being an opaque 1024-byte-period-encrypted blob cuts both ways. It means a Linux tool needs no key and can stream the resource verbatim — genuinely feasible. It also means the tool can never sanity-check what it is sending: it cannot verify the version, the target model, or that it grabbed the right resource. The presence of a second, unreferenced FWFILE resource of identical size (id 135) is a live foot-gun; nothing but the disassembly tells you 134 is the right one.

The biggest avoidable hazard is not the flash at all, it is device selection. The dongle (3367:1970), the mouse application (3367:1972) and the bootloader (3367:1971) all expose the same vendor collection 0xFF01/0x02 and the same report IDs 0xA0/0xA1. PROTOCOL.md section 1 correctly tells a CONFIG client to match on usage page and usage rather than PID — that advice is actively dangerous for a flasher. Any flashing code must hard-require VID:PID == 3367:1972 before it ever sends A0 3A, and 3367:1971 before it sends A0 03 / A0 06 / A0 09, and refuse outright on 3367:1970. Streaming 205 KB of mouse firmware into the dongle would brick all wireless use of the mouse and the dongle is a different chip with a different bootloader vendor (22D4), so the mouse updater could not recover it.

Two operational notes. A successful update ends with A1 13 = factory reset, so the user's entire configuration is wiped; back up the 1024-byte config blob with egg-cli before flashing. And since there is no version gate, do not deliberately interrupt the flash to test recoverability during the Windows capture — take one clean end-to-end trace first; the capture can be repeated afterwards, a bricked mouse cannot.

My recommendation on shape: do not write a general-purpose flasher. Write a strict replayer of the captured session — fixed 205 blocks from resource 134, fixed framing, hard VID/PID gates, abort on any unexpected status — and keep the Windows updater as the documented recovery path. The one item that makes or breaks this and cannot be obtained any other way is the bootloader's own HID report descriptor, so make capturing 3367:1971's full descriptors the top priority of the Windows session.

result.question: Could the firmware payload be located RELIABLY across future/other versions of the updater — i.e. without hardcoding a byte offset?
result.answer:
# Short answer

Yes — the payload is a **PE resource**, not appended data, so a standard PE parser on Linux locates it with no fixed offset and gets its length from the resource directory. The vendor's own code does exactly the same (`SizeofResource`), so there is no length constant anywhere to drift out of sync.

But there is one genuinely fragile part, and it is worse than "a hardcoded ID": **v1.10 ships TWO firmware images and only sends one of them.** Any naive "grab the FWFILE resource" extractor is a coin flip on this sample.

---

## 1. Exact resource identity (PROVEN, this sample)

```
type     = "FWFILE"   (string/named type, UTF-16 in the resource dir)
name     = 134        (integer, = 0x86)    <-- the one actually flashed
name     = 135        (integer, = 0x87)    <-- present, NEVER loaded
language = 2052       (0x0804, zh-CN) for both
size     = 209920 bytes (0x33400) for both, identical
```

So the pefile/LIEF tuple is `('FWFILE', 134, 2052)`. Extractable on Linux with `pefile`, `LIEF`, `pev`, or ~60 lines of Python stdlib — no Windows, no Ghidra.

**Not appended data.** End of last section = 0x25DE00 = exact file size ⇒ **overlay is 0 bytes**. The SECURITY data directory is `(0,0)` ⇒ not Authenticode-signed, so nothing is appended at all. Same for the config tool. No magic/header hunting needed, and none exists: the payload's first bytes are `b2 06 aa d6 5b ca 25 f8` — not zlib, gzip, zstd, lzma or lz4.

**No length or offset is stored anywhere else.** A scalar scan for `0x33400` (209920) and `0xCD` (205) found zero relevant hits. The loader takes the length purely from `SizeofResource()`:

```
004041ac  CALL [SizeofResource]
004041b9  SHR ECX,0xa          ; record count = size >> 10
004041bc  MOV [EDI+0x25c],ECX
004041c2  SHL ECX,0xa
004041c5  SUB EBX,ECX          ; remainder = size & 0x3FF (zero-padded to 1024)
```

That is the ideal situation: the only source of truth for both position and length is the resource directory, which is exactly what a Linux parser reads.

## 2. The fragile part: which resource ID

`FUN_004040f0 @ 0x004040f0` is the **only** site in the binary that references the `L"FWFILE"` literal, and the ID is an immediate:

```
00404190  68 f0 ad 59 00     PUSH 0x59adf0    ; L"FWFILE"
00404195  68 86 00 00 00     PUSH 0x86        ; <-- resource ID 134, HARDCODED
0040419a  6a 00              PUSH 0x0         ; hModule = NULL (own image)
0040419c  ff 15 98 72 56 00  CALL [FindResourceW]
```

No `EnumResourceNames*`/`EnumResourceTypes*` are imported at all, and `FindResourceExW` is used only once, in unrelated MFC code (`0x004b1e94`). Every other `PUSH 0x86`/`PUSH 0x87` in the image is MFC noise (`OnToolHitTest`, `UpdateDialogControls`, …).

So **resource 135 is dead in v1.10**. Its purpose is **unknown**. What I can say is that 134 and 135 have *identical structure* — same 209920 bytes, same 135 distinct 1024-byte records, same erased band at records 133–203, same distinct final record — i.e. two builds with the same flash layout. Plausibly two hardware revisions or an old/new pair. Flashing 135 would be flashing something the vendor tool never sends to anything.

Consequences for a Linux extractor:
- "take the only FWFILE resource" → **fails here** (there are two)
- "take the highest ID" → picks **135**, which is never flashed
- "take the largest" → tie
- MFC resource IDs are editor-assigned from 128 up, so a future build could easily renumber to 136.

## 3. The second sample does NOT confirm a firmware convention

The `USBDATA` resource in the config tools is **not** a firmware payload:

- `type="USBDATA", name=165, lang=2052`, 90112 bytes (0x16000)
- starts `4d 5a 90 00` — it is a **complete 32-bit PE**, i386, 5 sections, `.reloc` ending exactly at 0x16000
- **byte-identical across all five config tools** (OP1w v1 1.03 & 1.04, OP1w v2 1.02, XM2w v1 1.03, XM2w v2 1.02): SHA-256 `db06d7af1f6322bbb1e5e52c6f0c8fd696945306023de367d35cdb7bae380830`
- its own resource tree contains **only a 346-byte MANIFEST** — no nested payload
- it imports `hid.dll` (`HidD_SetFeature`/`GetFeature`/…), carries hidapi symbol names, and the strings `VID_22D4`, `PID_1502`, `PID_1503`, `MI_00`, `Firmware_update_progress`, `Get_fw_version`

So it is the dropped **dongle-updater engine**, with the bootloader VID/PID `22D4:1502/1503`, and it ships no firmware image of its own.

What this confirms: the vendor's *packaging habit* — big blobs go into a custom string-named resource type, integer ID, language 2052. What it does **not** confirm: a stable firmware-payload layout. **n is still 1 for firmware payloads.** I cannot demonstrate cross-version stability from a single updater; that claim is unverified, not merely uncertain.

## 4. Recommended extraction method (offset-free, and it disambiguates the ID)

I wrote and tested it: `C:\Users\jmeyer\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-jmeyer-Downloads-endgame\d4a5925e-1f26-4c72-9f6c-eba7bd4a2bae\scratchpad\q_locate\extract_fw.py` (with `pelib.py` alongside). Stdlib only, no Ghidra, runs on Linux.

Recover the ID **from the code**, not from the resource tree, by matching the call sequence:

```
68 <LE32 VA of L"FWFILE\0">    PUSH string
68 <LE32 id>                   PUSH resource id     <-- read this
6a 00                          PUSH 0
ff 15 <LE32 IAT slot>          CALL [FindResourceW]
```

The literal's VA is itself found by searching for `"FWFILE\0"` UTF-16 in `.rdata` and mapping raw→RVA→VA. Tested output:

```
FWFILE res : [('134','2052',209920), ('135','2052',209920)]
code sites : [('rva 0x4190', 'id 134', 'thunk 0x567298')]
SELECTED   : type=FWFILE id=134 lang=2052 size=209920 rva=0x1D91E8
  sha256   : ad612be22f77907162429e1053a6fad53c91bd59a7f0916c9715970e56aa2b27
  entropy  : 7.9788   looks-PE: False
  records  : 205 x 1024 (+0 remainder)   distinct: 135, most-repeated x71
```

Two rules that matter: **match the type name and take the size from the resource directory** (never a constant), and **refuse to run if the code scan does not pin exactly one ID**. Fail loudly rather than guess — that is the difference between "no update" and "bricked mouse".

Caveat on the scan: it assumes this exact instruction encoding. A recompile with different optimisation could push the args differently, and then the scan returns 0 sites and (correctly) refuses.

## 5. How to validate an extraction

Cheap, local:
- length from the directory, `size % 4 == 0`; expect 209920 for v1.10
- SHA-256 `ad612be2…` for v1.10 / id 134
- entropy ≈ 7.98 bits/byte; reject `MZ`, reject any compression magic, reject H < 7.5
- record shape: 205 × 1024, records 133–203 (0x21400–0x32FFF) byte-identical, record 204 distinct

That record shape is itself informative: **71 identical 1024-byte records at full entropy proves block-wise encryption at exactly 1024-byte granularity with no chaining across records, and rules out compression** (a compressor would not emit 71 identical incompressible kilobytes). Between images 134 and 135 those same records differ, so key or IV varies per image. Mode is otherwise **unknown** — longest common prefix between distinct records is 1 byte, consistent with random, so I cannot distinguish ECB/CBC-fixed-IV/whitened.

Decisive, and it comes free with the one-shot capture:
- **The host never transforms the bytes.** Instruction-verified in both copy loops — `0x00404250`–`0x004042a4` is a plain `MOVZX`/`MOV` byte copy, and `0x004026a4` is a bare `MOVSD.REP` of 0x100 dwords. No XOR, no table lookup, no arithmetic. The device decrypts; the host is a pipe.
- Therefore the payload bytes on the wire **must equal the resource bytes verbatim** at packet offset +16. Diff the capture against `FWFILE_134.bin`: a byte-for-byte match proves both the extraction and the ID choice end-to-end for that version, and proves no key is needed on the Linux side.
- Each record packet (`FUN_00402640 @ 0x00402640`) is report `0xA0` / 1041 bytes: `[1]=0x06`, `[2..3]` = record index u16 LE, `[4..5]` = **16-bit additive sum of payload bytes [16..1039]** (stored at `0x004026ff`/`0x0040270e`), `[16..1039]` = the 1024 payload bytes. So the device does check per-record integrity, and a reimplementation computes the same sum trivially.
evidence: Payload is a PE resource, not appended data: updater .rsrc raw 0x1B9800..0x23CC00, RESOURCE data dir = rva 0x001C0000 size 0x00083380; end of last section 0x25DE00 == file size 0x25DE00, so overlay = 0 bytes; SECURITY data directory = (0,0) i.e. no Authenticode blob appended.

Resource identity: type="FWFILE" (string name), name=134, language=2052, size=209920 (0x33400), rva=0x001D91E8, raw 0x1D29E8. Second entry: type="FWFILE", name=135, language=2052, size=209920, rva=0x0020C5E8, raw 0x205DE8. Exactly two entries, both lang 2052.

ID is hardcoded and only 134 is used. FUN_004040f0 @ 0x004040f0, the sole xref to the L"FWFILE" literal at VA 0x0059ADF0: 00404190 `68 f0 ad 59 00 PUSH 0x59adf0`; 00404195 `68 86 00 00 00 PUSH 0x86`; 0040419a `6a 00 PUSH 0x0`; 0040419c `ff 15 98 72 56 00 CALL [FindResourceW]`. Resource 135 (0x87) never reaches FindResourceW — all PUSH 0x87 sites are MFC (OnToolHitTest 0x00413370, UpdateDialogControls 0x00414c94, FUN_0043c2f1 0x0043c39c, FUN_0043c56f 0x0043c5a4, FUN_0040de37 0x0040de79).
No enumeration fallback: EnumResourceNamesW/A and EnumResourceTypesW are not imported at all; FindResourceExW has one caller, FUN_004b1e11 @ site 0x004b1e94 (MFC), unrelated to FWFILE.

Length comes only from the resource directory, never a constant: 004041ac CALL [SizeofResource]; 004041b9 `c1 e9 0a SHR ECX,0xa` (records = size>>10); 004041bc MOV [EDI+0x25c],ECX; 004041c2 SHL ECX,0xa; 004041c5 SUB EBX,ECX (remainder = size & 0x3FF, zero-padded via memset(...,0,0x400)). A FindConst scan for 0x33400 (209920) and 0xCD (205) returned no relevant hits.

Host applies NO transform (instruction-verified): loader copy loop 0x00404250-0x004042a4 is MOVZX EAX,byte ptr[..] / MOV byte ptr[..],AL only; per-record sender copy at 0x004026a4 is `f3 a5 MOVSD.REP ES:EDI,ESI` with ECX=0x100 (1024 bytes). No XOR, no table lookup, no arithmetic on payload bytes.

Per-record packet (FUN_00402640 @ 0x00402640): 0x00402682 `MOV word [EBP-0x414+..],0x6a0` -> [0]=0xA0,[1]=0x06; 0x00402655/0x00402664 write ECX low/high byte to buffer offsets 2 and 3 (record index u16 LE); checksum loop 0x004026b0-0x004026e5 sums bytes over buffer offsets 0x10..0x40F into 16-bit SI; stored at offsets 4 and 5 by 0x004026ff `MOV byte [EBP+0xfffffbec],AL` and 0x0040270e `MOV byte [EBP+0xfffffbed],AL`; 0x004026fa `MOV EDX,0x411` = 1041-byte report.

Second sample is NOT firmware: "USBDATA"/165/2052, 90112 bytes (0x16000), begins 4d 5a 90 00 = a complete i386 PE (.text 0xF29A, .rdata 0x3B9E, .data 0x1C20, .rsrc 0x1B4, .reloc 0x1A82 ending exactly at 0x16000). Its only resource is a 346-byte MANIFEST/2/1033 — no nested payload. Byte-identical in all five config tools: SHA-256 db06d7af1f6322bbb1e5e52c6f0c8fd696945306023de367d35cdb7bae380830. Contains hid.dll imports (HidD_SetFeature/GetFeature/GetAttributes/GetHidGuid/GetPreparsedData), hidapi symbol names, and strings VID_22D4, PID_1502, PID_1503, MI_00, Firmware_update_progress, Get_fw_version at offsets 0x11A38/0x11A4C/0x11A60/0x11A6C/0x12FDA/0x1303B.

Payload is encrypted at 1024-byte granularity, not compressed: 205 records of 1024; records 133..203 (offsets 0x21400..0x32FFF) byte-identical (71 records); record 204 distinct; 135 distinct records total; whole-blob entropy 7.9788 (134) / 7.9791 (135); first bytes b2 06 aa d6 (no zlib/gzip/zstd/lzma/lz4 magic). Shift-8192 and shift-1024 self-XOR over the head give H=7.9986/7.9966 and ~0.39% zeros, ruling out a periodic additive keystream. Images 134 and 135 share 0 aligned 16-byte blocks and agree on only 0.49% of bytes, so key/IV differs per image. Both images have identical record structure (135 distinct, repeats at 133..203), i.e. the same flash layout.

Tested offset-free extractor that recovers the ID from code: C:\Users\jmeyer\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-jmeyer-Downloads-endgame\d4a5925e-1f26-4c72-9f6c-eba7bd4a2bae\scratchpad\q_locate\extract_fw.py (+ pelib.py). Output: code sites [('rva 0x4190','id 134','thunk 0x567298')]; SELECTED type=FWFILE id=134 lang=2052 size=209920 rva=0x1D91E8; sha256 ad612be22f77907162429e1053a6fad53c91bd59a7f0916c9715970e56aa2b27; entropy 7.9788; 205 x 1024 records, +0 remainder.

Updater VERSION resource: FileDescription/ProductName "Endgame Gear OP1w 4k Firmware Updater", FileVersion 1.1.0.0. Bootloader-related UTF-16 strings at rva 0x19AEE6 'bldr request failed', 0x19AF1A 'bldr device request failed', 0x19AF8E 'bldr start request failed', 0x19B012 'bldr complete request failed'. The updater contains no VID_/PID_ literal strings (unlike the config tools).

Sample scope: exactly one updater binary exists locally (C:\Users\jmeyer\Downloads\endgame\OP1w4k\Endgame_Gear_OP1w_4k_Firmware_Updater_v1.10-660998ec.exe, 2481664 bytes). No second updater version was available, so no cross-version comparison of the FWFILE layout or ID was possible.
result.risk_note:
The location problem is the safe part; the selection problem is not.

1. Offset fragility is a non-issue. Position and length both come from the PE resource directory, which is what the vendor tool itself uses (SizeofResource). No byte offset needs hardcoding, and there is no length constant in the binary to drift.

2. The real brick risk is picking the wrong FWFILE. v1.10 ships 134 and 135, identical in size and structure, and only 134 is ever sent. "The FWFILE resource" is ambiguous on the only sample that exists. Resource 135's purpose is UNKNOWN — it could be another hardware revision. An extractor must pin the ID from the code and hard-refuse if it cannot, rather than defaulting to any heuristic.

3. Cross-version stability is UNVERIFIED, not just uncertain. With one updater binary I cannot show that the type name, the ID, the record size or the encryption stay put. The ID is an immediate an MFC resource editor assigns; renumbering between releases is entirely ordinary. Every future updater must be re-checked, not assumed.

4. Good news that materially lowers risk: the host never transforms the payload (instruction-verified in both copy loops). The device decrypts. So a Linux tool does not need to break the encryption — only to extract the resource byte-exactly and stream it in 1024-byte records with the 16-bit additive sum at +4. And the one-shot Windows capture will prove the extraction: if the bytes at packet offset +16 match FWFILE_134.bin verbatim, both the extraction and the ID choice are confirmed end-to-end.

5. Separate flag, outside my question but it bears on bricking: this updater's VERSION resource says "Endgame Gear OP1w 4k Firmware Updater" (the v1 model), while CLAUDE.md states the project's hardware is the OP1w 4k v2 and that only the v2 has ever been tested. PROTOCOL.md §10 notes the shared 3367:1970 dongle means the dongle PID does not identify the mouse. Whether this v1 image is safe for the user's actual mouse is not something I examined and should not be assumed — the presence of two images in one updater makes model/revision gating exactly the kind of thing to establish before any write.

6. The device's own acceptance criteria are unknown. Per-record 16-bit sums are host-computed; whether the bootloader verifies a whole-image signature, and what it does with a rejected image, is not established here. There is no evidence of a host-side rollback path.
